subject: Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 12 periods = 480 minutes
Total: 12 periods · 8h 0min

periods.activity_title: Breath, Wind, and the Air Around Us
periods.activity_description: Students perform the breath-holding exercise from Activity 11.1 to experience oxygen dependence directly, then construct a paper firki from Activity 11.2 and observe it spinning in moving air, connecting their observation to the concept of wind as moving air.

roles.role_description: Guides the breathing exercise, distributes paper for firki construction, and facilitates whole-class sharing of observations.
Perform the breath-holding exercise and record the sensation, then construct and test their own firki.

time_bands.activity: Students attempt to hold their breath and note the discomfort; they share observations and the teacher establishes that the body constantly needs oxygen from air.
Students follow step-by-step instructions to fold and pin a paper firki, then blow on it or move it through the air to observe rotation.
Students describe in their notebooks what made the firki spin and connect this to the idea that moving air is called wind.
Teacher draws out that air is a mixture of gases (nitrogen 78%, oxygen 21%, other gases 1%) and previews that this unit begins a chapter-long survey of nature's resources.

periods.teacher_notes: This opening unit anchors the chapter in the most immediately felt natural resource — the air students are breathing right now. Watch for the common confusion that air and wind are different substances rather than the same mixture in motion; the firki directly addresses this by making wind visible as moving air. If some students finish the firki quickly, ask them to predict whether the firki would spin faster near an open window — this probing question signals readiness to move on.
materials: Pencils or straw sticks for firki handles

periods.activity_title: Mapping Water: Where It Is and Where It Goes
periods.activity_description: Students examine a classroom-drawn sketch of the Earth's water distribution, identify saline versus freshwater sources, and then work through Activity 11.3 by listing daily household activities to discover how freshwater is used and wasted.

roles.role_description: Draws a simple pie-sketch on the board showing ocean water versus freshwater fractions and poses guiding questions about daily water use.
Collaboratively list household activities in a table, mark whether each wastes water, and suggest one conservation action per activity.

time_bands.activity: Teacher sketches the Earth's water distribution on the board; students note that about two-thirds of the surface is water yet most is saline and unfit for drinking or agriculture.
Groups work through Activity 11.3, listing activities such as hand washing, cooking, and gardening, marking wasteful steps, and proposing conservation alternatives.
Groups share their tables; the class builds a combined list of conservation strategies including turning off taps, fixing leaks, recycling, and rainwater harvesting.
Teacher briefly introduces stepwells — Bawadi in Rajasthan and Vav in Gujarat — as examples of traditional rainwater harvesting, setting up further exploration in the next unit.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit continues the first-stage survey begun in the previous unit by shifting from air to water; students are now observing a second major resource and recording its properties and distribution. A common error here is believing that because water covers so much of the Earth's surface there must be plenty of freshwater — the saline-versus-freshwater distinction is central and worth pausing on. The group table format encourages every student to contribute an activity they know from home, which broadens participation across different household contexts.
materials: Blackboard or chart paper for the water-distribution sketch

periods.activity_title: Sun, Forests, Soil, and Rocks — A First Survey
periods.activity_description: Students are guided through a structured survey of the remaining resources introduced in the chapter — solar energy, forests, soil and rocks, minerals, and fossil fuels — recording key observed properties and uses for each in a resource-survey table.

roles.role_description: Leads the class through each resource section in turn, using the board to model how to fill in the survey table.
Maintain a personal resource-survey table with columns for resource name, observable properties, and at least two uses.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces solar energy: sunlight enables photosynthesis, powers solar panels, cookers, and water heaters; students fill in the solar row of their table.

Teacher covers forests — dense plant communities providing habitat and food — then soil and rocks, noting Activity 11.4 observations about colour and texture differences between soil samples from different places; students fill in their rows.

Teacher introduces minerals extracted from rocks (aluminium, gold, copper, iron) and fossil fuels (petroleum, natural gas, coal) formed from ancient organisms; students complete the remaining rows of their survey table.
Students share one surprising fact from their table with a partner; teacher collects a few responses and frames the question: are all these resources equally easy to replace?

periods.teacher_notes: This unit completes the first-stage survey so that every resource the chapter addresses has been encountered before deeper analysis begins in the next stage. A common misconception to watch for is that fossil fuels are a form of solar energy — while ultimately true at a deep level, the chapter treats fossil fuels separately from solar energy, and conflating them will interfere with the renewable/non-renewable classification in a later unit. The closing question about replaceability is deliberately unresolved here; it is the seed for Stage 2.
materials: Student notebooks with a prepared or hand-drawn survey table (six rows: air, water, solar energy, forests, soil/rocks/minerals, fossil fuels)

periods.stage_label: Classify resources by replenishment and availability
periods.activity_title: How Long Does It Take? Sorting by Time to Replenish
periods.activity_description: Students investigate the replenishment timescales of each surveyed resource — seconds to hours for air, days to decades for forests, thousands to millions of years for soil and fossil fuels — and sort resources into fast-replenishing and slow-or-never-replenishing groups before the renewable/non-renewable definition is introduced.

roles.role_description: Poses the inquiry question 'How long would nature take to replace this if it were all used up?' and provides sentence starters to scaffold student reasoning.
Discuss each resource from their survey table and sort them onto a two-column poster labelled 'replenishes quickly' and 'replenishes slowly or not at all'.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the inquiry question and students revisit their survey tables from the previous unit to recall properties before beginning the sort.
Groups discuss each resource and place it in one of the two columns, citing evidence from what they already know — rain refills rivers, but coal took millions of years to form.
Groups share their sorted lists; the class notices disagreements (e.g., soil — thousands of years is slow, but forests can regrow in decades) and debates where to place contested resources.
Teacher introduces the formal terms 'renewable' and 'non-renewable' as names for the two columns the class just created, anchoring the definition in students' own sorting work.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens Stage 2 by driving the classification question from students' own inquiry rather than from a definition given upfront; the previous unit planted the seed with the closing question about replaceability. Watch for the frequent confusion that 'renewable' means 'available in large quantities' — students may place fossil fuels in the renewable column because there seems to be a lot of petrol at petrol stations; the timescale framing corrects this. Groups that reach confident agreement quickly can be challenged to think about where soil belongs — it is listed as non-renewable even though it forms naturally.
materials: Student survey tables from the previous unit
Large sheets of paper or chart paper for the two-column poster

periods.stage_label: Classify resources by replenishment and availability
periods.activity_title: Soil Samples Speak: Observing Variation Across Sources
periods.activity_description: Students carry out Activity 11.4 by observing soil samples collected from different locations, recording colour, texture, and visible materials under a magnifying lens, and explaining why soils differ based on the types of rock and organic matter present at each site.

roles.role_description: Distributes prepared soil samples and magnifying lenses, and circulates to prompt students to connect observed differences to the chapter's explanation of soil formation.
Observe, sketch, and record differences between soil samples in a table, then write one sentence explaining why the samples differ.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects this unit to the previous one: soils are classified as non-renewable because they take thousands of years to form from the disintegration of rocks by the Sun, water, and living organisms.

Groups observe their soil samples with the naked eye and magnifying lens, recording colour, texture, and visible particles in a four-column table (sample location, colour, texture, visible materials).
Groups write a sentence explaining why their samples look different, drawing on the idea that soil composition depends on the parent rock and organic matter at each site.
Teacher collects responses and reinforces that the variation observed is evidence that soil is a locally formed, slow-replenishing resource — not a uniform substance available everywhere.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit gives the non-renewable classification of soil a concrete, observable basis — students are not just accepting the label but seeing that soils differ because they form slowly and locally from specific parent rocks. Watch for students recording only colour and ignoring texture or visible organic material; prompt them to rub a pinch of soil between their fingers and note whether it feels gritty, smooth, or sticky. The sentence-writing step is a checkpoint: if students can link observed differences to formation process, they are ready to move to fossil fuels in the next unit.
materials: Soil samples from 3–4 different locations (prepared in small labelled bags or plates)

periods.stage_label: Classify resources by replenishment and availability
periods.activity_title: Fuel Survey: What Powers the Vehicles Around Us?
periods.activity_description: Students conduct Activity 11.5 by pooling a neighbourhood vehicle fuel survey, then classify each fuel type as renewable or non-renewable, noting that petrol, diesel, CNG, and coal all derive from fossil fuels — formed over millions of years and finite in quantity.

roles.role_description: Facilitates the pooling of individual survey results onto the board and guides the class in identifying which fuels are fossil-fuel-derived.
Contribute their observed vehicle-fuel pairs to the class tally and classify each fuel type using the renewable/non-renewable framework from the previous two units.

time_bands.activity: Students share vehicle-fuel observations from their neighbourhood; the teacher tallies fuel types on the board — petrol, diesel, CNG, electric, cycle — to build a class dataset.
Students classify each fuel type in their notebooks as renewable or non-renewable, citing the formation timescale and the fact that burning fossil fuels releases smoke and carbon dioxide.

Class discusses the classification of electric vehicles — electricity itself is not a natural resource, but the source matters: coal-powered electricity is non-renewable at its source while solar-powered electricity is renewable.
Teacher closes by noting that fossil fuel use creates both a supply problem (finite quantities) and an environmental problem (air pollution), previewing the evaluation work of the next stage.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit completes the classification stage by applying the renewable/non-renewable framework to the most visible non-renewable resource in students' daily lives — the fuels in vehicles they pass every day. A common confusion is treating CNG as renewable because it is a gas and seems cleaner than petrol; the chapter is clear that CNG is a fossil fuel and therefore non-renewable. The electric vehicle discussion is genuinely ambiguous and worth holding open — it models that classification sometimes depends on tracing a resource back to its source.
homework: Record the types of fuel used by the cooking and lighting in your home and classify each as renewable or non-renewable, giving one reason for your classification.

periods.stage_label: Explain causal mechanisms linking resource use to environmental impact
periods.activity_title: Why Burning Fossil Fuels Harms the Air We Breathe
periods.activity_description: Students examine the causal chain from fossil fuel combustion to air pollution: burning releases smoke and carbon dioxide, which degrade the air quality established in Stage 1 as essential for life, linking back to the breath-holding experience from the first unit of this plan.

roles.role_description: Explains the combustion-to-pollution causal chain using the board and draws an explicit connection back to the air composition data from the chapter's opening section.
Construct a cause-and-effect diagram in their notebooks showing the chain from fossil fuel use to air pollution to impact on living beings.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps the classification work of the previous units: fossil fuels are non-renewable and finite; today the class examines what happens when they are burned.

Teacher explains the combustion chain step by step — fossil fuel burned → smoke and carbon dioxide released → air quality changes → impacts on breathing and climate; students draw this as an annotated arrow diagram.
Students extend their diagram by adding a second causal chain for deforestation: fewer trees → less carbon dioxide absorbed → more carbon dioxide in air → compounding the combustion effect.
Brief pair-share: each student names one action described in the chapter that interrupts one of the two chains, setting up the conservation-evaluation work ahead.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens Stage 3 by showing students that the resources they classified are not independent — burning fossil fuels damages air, and losing forests amplifies that damage, so the two chains are connected. Watch for students treating air pollution as a simple smell problem rather than a change in the gas composition that the chapter established in Section 11.1; the oxygen and carbon dioxide proportions are the relevant quantities. The pair-share interruption exercise is a first step toward the evaluative reasoning that defines the final stage.

periods.stage_label: Explain causal mechanisms linking resource use to environmental impact
periods.activity_title: Forests Fall, Soil Erodes: Tracing the Ecological Chain
periods.activity_description: Students investigate the causal link between deforestation and soil degradation: tree roots hold soil, fallen leaves enrich it, and without forest cover soil loses nutrients and becomes vulnerable to erosion — a chain that ultimately reduces the land's capacity to support life.

roles.role_description: Poses the inquiry question 'What happens to soil when a forest disappears?' and guides students through the evidence available in the chapter.
Construct a sequence diagram tracing the steps from deforestation to soil degradation, citing chapter evidence at each step.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the inquiry question and asks groups to recall from their survey tables what forests provide to soil — fallen leaves decompose and enrich the soil with nutrients.
Groups construct a four-step sequence diagram: trees cut → leaf litter stops → soil nutrient cycle broken AND roots gone → soil exposed to erosion by wind and water.
Groups extend their diagram by adding the human response: Chipko movement, Van Mahotsav tree planting, and the decades-long timescale needed to restore a forest.
Teacher connects this chain to the soil classification from Stage 2 — soil is non-renewable on human timescales, so once eroded it is not quickly replaced, compounding the loss.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit deepens the causal reasoning begun in the previous unit by showing that resource degradation chains are interconnected — losing forests accelerates the degradation of soil, another non-renewable resource. A misconception to watch for is the idea that soil regenerates quickly once trees are replanted; the chapter is explicit that soil formation takes thousands of years, so even successful reforestation does not immediately restore eroded soil. Groups that finish their sequence diagrams early can be asked to add an arrow showing how restored forests eventually slow further soil loss — this adds a feedback dimension.

periods.stage_label: Explain causal mechanisms linking resource use to environmental impact
periods.activity_title: Solar Energy's Role: From Photosynthesis to Food Chains
periods.activity_description: The teacher demonstrates the indirect dependence of all organisms on solar energy by tracing a food chain on the board — starting from the cow-grazing scenario in the chapter — and students identify where in the chain solar energy enters and how removing it collapses the whole system.

roles.role_description: Constructs the food chain demonstration on the board step by step, pausing at each link to ask students what happens if that link is broken.
Draw the food chain in their notebooks, annotate where solar energy enters, and write one sentence explaining why solar energy is called the foundational energy source for all life.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws the cow-grazing scenario on the board: Sun → grass (photosynthesis) → cow (grazes) → human (drinks milk or eats beef); students copy and label each arrow with the type of energy transfer.
Teacher removes the Sun from the chain and asks: what happens to the grass? Then removes the grass: what happens to the cow? Students trace the collapse and annotate their diagrams.

Students extend their diagram to include a solar panel on a rooftop — Sun → solar panel → electricity → appliance — and label this as a direct use of solar energy, contrasting it with the indirect biological chain.

Students write their explanatory sentence; a few are shared aloud and the teacher reinforces that solar energy is renewable and that its mechanisms (photosynthesis, direct capture) are themselves a form of conservation.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit completes Stage 3's causal-mechanism work by showing that the most fundamental resource — solar energy — underpins all others; the food-chain demonstration makes this visible rather than abstract. A common confusion here is between direct and indirect solar energy use, which the chapter explicitly addresses through the cow scenario; make sure students annotate both pathways in their diagrams so the distinction is preserved. The connection back to the renewable classification from Stage 2 — solar energy replenishes daily — prepares students for the evaluative comparisons of the next stage.
homework: Trace the chain of resources used to make one meal at your home (e.g., breakfast) and identify whether each resource in the chain is renewable or non-renewable.

periods.stage_label: Evaluate conservation choices and develop informed judgements about responsible consumption
periods.activity_title: Every Daily Activity Draws on Nature's Treasures
periods.activity_description: Students work through Activity 11.6 by tracing the natural resources embedded in everyday activities — washing clothes, making clay toys, cooking breakfast — then evaluate which resource dependencies could be reduced or shifted to a renewable alternative.

roles.role_description: Introduces Activity 11.6 and models the tracing process for one activity before groups take over.
Trace the resource chain for at least three daily activities and evaluate for each whether a conservation action or renewable substitute is available.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the tracing process for 'cooking breakfast': food (agricultural land needs water and soil) + fuel (gas — fossil fuel) + utensils (metals extracted from minerals — non-renewable).

Groups trace resource chains for washing clothes, making a clay toy, and one activity of their choice, completing a table with columns: activity, resources used, renewable or non-renewable, possible conservation action.

Groups share their conservation actions; the class evaluates which actions genuinely reduce dependence (e.g., solar cooking replaces fossil fuel) versus which only reduce waste (e.g., turning off a tap).
Teacher introduces the Gandhian quote — 'Earth provides enough to satisfy every man's need but not for every man's greed' — as a framing device for the evaluation criteria the class just developed.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens Stage 4 by grounding the evaluation task in the daily activities students already know, building directly on the causal-chain reasoning of the previous stage. A misconception to watch for is treating all conservation actions as equally effective — students may list 'don't waste water' and 'switch to solar cooking' as equivalent, but the second actually shifts resource type while the first only reduces quantity; the class evaluation discussion should surface this distinction. The Gandhian quote is in the chapter and works well here as a memorable criterion: need versus greed as a test for any consumption decision.
materials: Student survey tables and resource chains from earlier units

periods.stage_label: Evaluate conservation choices and develop informed judgements about responsible consumption
periods.activity_title: Human-Made vs. Natural Resources: Drawing the Boundary
periods.activity_description: Students examine the chapter's distinction between natural resources — provided directly by nature — and human-made resources created from natural resources, then evaluate whether labelling a resource 'human-made' reduces or conceals its dependence on non-renewable inputs.

roles.role_description: Explains the natural versus human-made resource distinction from Section 11.7 and poses the evaluative question about hidden dependencies.
Sort a given list of ten items into natural and human-made, then for each human-made item identify the natural resource it depends on and classify that source as renewable or non-renewable.

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains Section 11.7's framework: natural resources are provided by nature; human-made resources are created by humans using natural resources — a mobile phone uses about a dozen minerals.

Students individually sort ten items (plastic bottle, wooden chair, glass window, solar panel, CNG bus, bread, cotton shirt, aluminium can, paper, tap water) into natural or human-made, then trace each human-made item to its natural resource source and classify that source.
Students compare their classifications with a partner, resolve disagreements, and notice that nearly every human-made item depends on at least one non-renewable natural resource.
Teacher draws the evaluative implication: calling something 'human-made' does not eliminate its resource footprint — responsible consumption requires tracing back to the source.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit extends the evaluation framework by showing that the natural/human-made distinction is not a reason to treat human-made items as resource-free; it is an invitation to trace dependencies. Watch for students classifying tap water as human-made because it comes through pipes — the chapter is clear that water is a natural resource, and pipes are the delivery system, not the source. The partner comparison is a checkpoint: students who can correctly trace a human-made item to a non-renewable natural resource source are demonstrating the evaluation reasoning targeted by this stage.
materials: Blackboard with the list of ten items

periods.stage_label: Evaluate conservation choices and develop informed judgements about responsible consumption
periods.activity_title: Judicious or Greedy? Evaluating Resource Decisions
periods.activity_description: Students evaluate a set of six resource-use scenarios drawn from the chapter — from Chipko to windmill farms to rainwater harvesting to fossil fuel dependence — judging each as responsible or irresponsible consumption and justifying their judgement using the chapter's renewable/non-renewable framework and the need-versus-greed criterion.

roles.role_description: Presents the six scenarios on the board and facilitates whole-class discussion of contested judgements.
Evaluate each scenario collaboratively, produce a written justification citing both the resource type and the conservation principle, and share their judgement with the class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents six scenarios on the board: (1) Muppandal windmill farm generating electricity; (2) clearing forest for farmland; (3) installing a Bawadi stepwell for rainwater harvesting; (4) using CNG instead of petrol in buses; (5) mining granite for construction; (6) using solar cookers in a village.

Groups evaluate each scenario, writing a two-part justification: (a) identify the resource type (renewable or non-renewable) and (b) judge whether this use is responsible or irresponsible given the chapter's conservation principles.

Groups share their judgements; the class debates contested cases — CNG is less polluting than petrol but still non-renewable; granite mining is destructive but rocks are used for construction cited in the chapter — and refines justifications.
Teacher closes the unit and the chapter by returning to the Gandhian quote, asking each student to silently identify one resource they personally use whose consumption they would now reconsider.

periods.teacher_notes: This closing unit completes the cognitive arc: students began by observing and describing resources, classified them by replenishment, explained how their misuse causes harm, and now evaluate real choices using those frameworks together. Watch for groups defaulting to 'all non-renewable use is bad' — the chapter does not support this absolute position; granite is non-renewable but its use in construction is presented as normal and legitimate, and the issue is responsible rather than zero use. The silent personal reflection at the close is not assessed but is drawn directly from the chapter's closing message about waste-free living.
materials: Student work from all previous units

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students perform hands-on observations of air, water, and other resources — including the breathing exercise, firki construction, water distribution mapping, and a structured survey of solar energy, forests, soil, rocks, and fossil fuels — recording key properties and uses for each.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can describe the observable properties and uses of at least five natural resources (air, water, solar energy, forests, soil/rocks/fossil fuels) drawing on direct experience or survey evidence.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Classify resources by replenishment and availability
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students sort resources by replenishment timescale through inquiry and hands-on activities — including soil-sample observation and a fuel survey — arriving at the renewable/non-renewable classification grounded in evidence rather than definition.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can classify a given natural resource as renewable or non-renewable and cite its replenishment timescale as evidence for that classification.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Explain causal mechanisms linking resource use to environmental impact
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students construct cause-and-effect diagrams tracing fossil fuel combustion to air pollution, deforestation to soil degradation, and the solar energy chain through photosynthesis to all life — explaining how resource misuse produces compounding environmental consequences.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can construct a causal chain showing how the overuse or destruction of at least one natural resource leads to a specific environmental impact, citing chapter evidence at each step.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Evaluate conservation choices and develop informed judgements about responsible consumption
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students trace natural resource dependencies in daily activities and human-made objects, then evaluate resource-use scenarios as responsible or irresponsible consumption by applying the renewable/non-renewable framework and the need-versus-greed conservation criterion.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can evaluate a resource-use scenario as responsible or irresponsible by classifying the resource type, tracing its impact chain, and justifying their judgement using the chapter's conservation principles.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe the observable properties and uses of at least five natural resources (air, water, solar energy, forests, soil/rocks/fossil fuels) drawing on direct experience or survey evidence.

competency.competency_text: Judicious consumption of resources and mitigation of climate change.

assessment_items.question_text: A student holds their breath during the breathing exercise from class. The discomfort they feel is because the body cannot function without which gas found in air?

options.label: A
options.text: Argon

options.label: B
options.text: Carbon dioxide

options.label: C
options.text: Nitrogen

options.label: D
options.text: Oxygen

what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses nitrogen (78% of air, the most abundant gas) with the gas the body actively uses; student may equate 'most of air' with 'most needed'.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses carbon dioxide — which the body produces and exhales — with the gas it requires; a reversal of the gas's role in respiration.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses argon — a trace inert gas mentioned in the 1% remainder — with a biologically essential gas, suggesting the student has not distinguished between gas proportions and biological necessity.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the gas-proportion data can still answer correctly by connecting the breath-holding experience directly to the concept of oxygen need, without recalling percentages. Providing the air composition data as a reference does not reduce the cognitive demand of identifying the essential gas.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe the observable properties and uses of at least five natural resources (air, water, solar energy, forests, soil/rocks/fossil fuels) drawing on direct experience or survey evidence.

competency.competency_text: Judicious consumption of resources and mitigation of climate change.

assessment_items.question_text: Although water covers about two-thirds of the Earth's surface, very little of it is available for drinking and agriculture. What is the main reason for this?

options.label: A
options.text: Most of Earth's water has already been used up by industries and cities.

options.label: B
options.text: Most of Earth's water is frozen in ice sheets and is permanently unavailable.

options.label: C
options.text: Most of Earth's water is saline, found in oceans and seas, and is not fit for drinking or agriculture.

options.label: D
options.text: Most of Earth's water is underground and cannot be reached.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Over-generalises from the chapter's mention of underground sources as one form of freshwater; student conflates 'hard to access' with 'most of the water', ignoring the saline-versus-freshwater distinction.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Applies a prior belief about industrial pollution or human consumption to explain scarcity rather than the physical distribution fact the chapter establishes.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Correctly identifies ice sheets as one form of freshwater but over-applies it — student has not distinguished between one freshwater form and the dominant reason freshwater is scarce (saline majority).

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can answer this question by reasoning from the water distribution sketch drawn in class, without relying solely on text recall. Allowing students to refer to their survey tables supports those who process information visually.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify resources by replenishment and availability
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify a given natural resource as renewable or non-renewable and cite its replenishment timescale as evidence for that classification.

competency.competency_text: Judicious consumption of resources and mitigation of climate change.

assessment_items.question_text: A student argues that coal is a renewable resource because new coal is forming underground right now. Which statement best explains why this argument is incorrect?

options.label: A
options.text: Coal is non-renewable because burning it releases smoke and carbon dioxide.

options.label: B
options.text: Coal is non-renewable because it exists in limited quantities in only a few countries.

options.label: C
options.text: Coal is not forming underground at all — it was only formed in the distant past.

options.label: D
options.text: Coal takes millions of years to form, so it cannot be replenished within a reasonable time frame relative to human use.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Shows the student has correctly rejected the 'renewable' label but has over-corrected to a factually wrong claim — coal formation did happen and continues geologically; the student has not grasped that the issue is timescale, not formation itself.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses the environmental impact of burning coal (pollution) with the criterion for classification as non-renewable (replenishment timescale); student is mixing two distinct ideas from the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses geographic distribution with replenishment rate; limited geographic occurrence is not the chapter's definition of non-renewable, which is specifically about time to replenish.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the abstract timescale concept can anchor their reasoning to the chapter's concrete examples: forests can regrow in decades, but coal took millions of years — comparing these two timescales makes the criterion concrete.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify resources by replenishment and availability
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify a given natural resource as renewable or non-renewable and cite its replenishment timescale as evidence for that classification.

competency.competency_text: Judicious consumption of resources and mitigation of climate change.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Resource | Time to replenish
Forest (after complete clearing) | Decades
Soil (from bare rock) | Thousands of years
Petroleum | Millions of years
Sunlight | Daily (continuous)
Groundwater (shallow aquifer) | Years to decades
assessment_items.question_text: Refer to the table provided. A student is sorting these resources into renewable and non-renewable. Which row is most likely to cause a sorting disagreement, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: Forest, because students might think trees never grow back after being cut.

options.label: B
options.text: Groundwater, because its replenishment time (years to decades) is long enough that some students will place it with non-renewables while others use the chapter's 'reasonable time frame' definition to call it renewable.

options.label: C
options.text: Petroleum, because students might think it forms faster than it does.

options.label: D
options.text: Sunlight, because some students confuse it with solar panels, which are human-made.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Shows students can identify petroleum as non-renewable but mislocates the source of classification difficulty — the petroleum timescale is unambiguously millions of years and unlikely to cause disagreement.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses a resource (sunlight) with a technology that captures it (solar panels); student is conflating the human-made/natural distinction with the renewable classification, a cross-concept error the chapter distinguishes explicitly.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Misreads the forest row — decades is clearly within a 'reasonable time frame' for renewable, and the chapter presents forests as renewable; student has over-applied non-renewable logic.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who need additional support can re-read the chapter's definition of 'reasonable time frame' and apply it row by row before choosing — the question rewards procedural application of the definition as much as intuitive classification.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify resources by replenishment and availability
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify a given natural resource as renewable or non-renewable and cite its replenishment timescale as evidence for that classification.

competency.competency_text: Judicious consumption of resources and mitigation of climate change.

assessment_items.question_text: During the fuel survey activity, a student recorded that their school bus runs on CNG. The student said: 'CNG is cleaner than petrol, so it must be a renewable resource.' Explain why the student's reasoning is incorrect, and classify CNG correctly using one piece of evidence from the chapter.
expected_elements: Identifies that 'cleaner' refers to pollution level, not to replenishment rate — these are two different properties of a resource.
States that CNG is a fossil fuel, formed from ancient organisms over millions of years.
Classifies CNG as non-renewable because it cannot be replenished within a reasonable time frame.
Distinguishes between environmental impact (less smoke) and resource classification (non-renewable based on formation timescale).

SCR.inclusivity: Students who express the classification verbally rather than in writing — for example, by pointing to the fuel survey tally and explaining aloud — are demonstrating the same reasoning. Written responses that use approximate scientific language ('takes a very long time to form') should be credited if the timescale reasoning is present.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain causal mechanisms linking resource use to environmental impact
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can construct a causal chain showing how the overuse or destruction of at least one natural resource leads to a specific environmental impact, citing chapter evidence at each step.

competency.competency_text: Judicious consumption of resources and mitigation of climate change.

assessment_items.question_text: A forest is completely cleared for farming. Which sequence correctly describes the causal chain of environmental impacts that follows, according to the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: Trees removed → animals lose habitat → soil immediately becomes more fertile from decaying wood → crop yields increase.

options.label: B
options.text: Trees removed → carbon dioxide in air decreases → photosynthesis slows across the region → food production drops at once.

options.label: C
options.text: Trees removed → leaf litter stops, roots gone → soil nutrients decrease and soil becomes exposed to erosion → land loses capacity to support life.

options.label: D
options.text: Trees removed → less oxygen produced → humans cannot breathe → all living things in the area die immediately.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Reverses the causal direction of decomposition — decaying wood does release nutrients, but the ongoing leaf-litter nutrient cycle stops when the forest is gone; student has applied a partial truth to reach an opposite conclusion.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Applies a correct principle (trees produce oxygen) but drastically over-extends the speed and severity of the consequence; student has not used the chapter's specific mechanism (leaf litter and root function) and has instead defaulted to a dramatic but non-chapter reasoning chain.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Reverses the carbon dioxide effect — removing trees would increase, not decrease, atmospheric carbon dioxide; this distractor catches students who know carbon dioxide is involved but have confused its direction of change.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can check each option against the sequence diagram they constructed in class — the activity produces a concrete artefact they can use as a reference framework for evaluating each chain.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain causal mechanisms linking resource use to environmental impact
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can construct a causal chain showing how the overuse or destruction of at least one natural resource leads to a specific environmental impact, citing chapter evidence at each step.

competency.competency_text: Judicious consumption of resources and mitigation of climate change.

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter describes burning fossil fuels and cutting forests as two separate problems. A student claims they are connected because cutting forests worsens the air-pollution impact of burning fossil fuels. Which explanation best supports this claim?

options.label: A
options.text: Cutting forests exposes more land, which absorbs more heat from the sun and warms the air, intensifying combustion.

options.label: B
options.text: Cutting forests means fewer trees to absorb the carbon dioxide released by burning fossil fuels, so the gas accumulates more rapidly in the air.

options.label: C
options.text: Cutting forests reduces the production of oxygen so completely that fossil fuels cannot burn efficiently.

options.label: D
options.text: Cutting forests releases stored fossil fuels buried under the roots, adding directly to the supply of combustible material.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Introduces a heat-absorption mechanism not supported by the chapter; student is reasoning from a real-world concept (albedo/land surface heating) that is outside the chapter's content, indicating they are importing knowledge rather than reasoning from the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Applies the correct principle that trees produce oxygen but extends it to an extreme and incorrect magnitude — the claim that oxygen reduction prevents combustion is not supported by the chapter and confuses atmospheric proportion with combustion chemistry.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses the biological origin of fossil fuels (ancient organisms buried underground) with a claim that living trees contain fossil fuels in their roots — a direct content confusion between how fossil fuels formed and where they are.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who constructed the two-chain diagram in class have a concrete visual tool they can apply here — the question is essentially asking them to draw an arrow between the two chains they already built.

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter states that 'it takes many years to grow a new forest or restore a lost one.' Using what you know about the role of forests in the soil nutrient cycle, explain why losing a forest causes damage that persists long after the trees are gone.
expected_elements: States that fallen leaves decompose on the forest floor and enrich the soil with nutrients, forming a continuous nutrient cycle.
Explains that when the forest is removed, this leaf-litter cycle stops and soil nutrients are no longer replenished.
Notes that tree roots hold soil in place, so their removal leaves soil exposed to erosion by wind and water.
Connects the slow formation of soil (thousands of years from rock disintegration) to why eroded soil cannot be quickly replaced even after replanting begins.
Concludes that the damage persists because soil — a non-renewable resource on human timescales — is lost faster than it can reform.

SCR.inclusivity: Students may present this explanation as a drawn sequence diagram with brief labels rather than continuous prose — both formats demonstrate the same causal reasoning. Students who mention only one mechanism (nutrient cycle or erosion but not both) should receive partial credit with a prompt to consider the role of roots.

assessment_items.stage_label: Evaluate conservation choices and develop informed judgements about responsible consumption
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can evaluate a resource-use scenario as responsible or irresponsible by classifying the resource type, tracing its impact chain, and justifying their judgement using the chapter's conservation principles.

competency.competency_text: Judicious consumption of resources and mitigation of climate change.

assessment_items.question_text: A village installs a solar cooker so that families no longer need to use wood or LPG for cooking. Which statement best evaluates the conservation impact of this change?

options.label: A
options.text: The change is irresponsible because concentrated sunlight from solar cookers could damage the environment.

options.label: B
options.text: The change is not a conservation measure because solar panels used in solar cookers are human-made and therefore consume natural resources to manufacture.

options.label: C
options.text: The change is only a small improvement because solar cookers work slowly and cannot replace all cooking needs.

options.label: D
options.text: The change shifts dependence from non-renewable fossil fuel and slow-replenishing wood to a renewable energy source, reducing resource depletion and avoiding air pollution from combustion.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Evaluates the technology's practical efficiency rather than its resource-classification impact; student is applying a usage-rate criterion rather than the chapter's renewable/non-renewable and pollution framework.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Applies the human-made resource concept from Section 11.7 but uses it to dismiss a genuine conservation gain; student has learned the natural/human-made distinction but has not grasped that the relevant evaluation criterion is the operational resource used, not the material of the device.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Invents an environmental harm not present in the chapter; the distractor catches students who apply a vague precautionary reasoning rather than evaluating against specific chapter criteria.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can structure their evaluation using the two-part framework practised in class: (a) identify the resource type shift and (b) assess the impact chain — this procedural scaffold is accessible to students who find open evaluation language difficult.

assessment_items.stage_label: Evaluate conservation choices and develop informed judgements about responsible consumption
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can evaluate a resource-use scenario as responsible or irresponsible by classifying the resource type, tracing its impact chain, and justifying their judgement using the chapter's conservation principles.

competency.competency_text: Judicious consumption of resources and mitigation of climate change.

assessment_items.question_text: Gandhi's quote at the end of the chapter says the Earth provides enough for every person's need but not for every person's greed. Which scenario from the chapter best illustrates the line between need and greed in resource use?

options.label: A
options.text: Building houses using granite and sandstone, because all construction is an example of greed.

options.label: B
options.text: Collecting soil from different locations for study, because any removal of natural resources is irresponsible.

options.label: C
options.text: Planting trees during Van Mahotsav, because adding more trees than currently exist is greedy use of land.

options.label: D
options.text: Using windmills to generate electricity rather than burning more coal to meet the same demand, because this meets the need for energy while reducing depletion of a non-renewable resource.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Over-extends the need/greed distinction to a blanket condemnation of rock use; the chapter explicitly presents construction using granite and sandstone as legitimate and cites specific monuments, so this distractor catches students who apply the conservation message too broadly.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Misapplies the greed concept to a conservation action; student has confused 'adding more than currently exists' with greed, failing to recognise that Van Mahotsav is presented as a restoration effort, not an excess.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Misapplies responsible use to a study activity; the chapter presents Activity 11.4 (collecting soil samples for observation) as a legitimate learning exercise, and the responsible-use principle targets wasteful extraction, not educational observation.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students may reason through this question by testing each option against the specific scenarios the chapter presents, rather than applying an abstract definition of greed — the chapter's examples are the anchor, and referencing them explicitly in reasoning is fully valid.

assessment_items.stage_label: Evaluate conservation choices and develop informed judgements about responsible consumption
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can evaluate a resource-use scenario as responsible or irresponsible by classifying the resource type, tracing its impact chain, and justifying their judgement using the chapter's conservation principles.

competency.competency_text: Judicious consumption of resources and mitigation of climate change.

assessment_items.question_text: A city government is choosing between two plans to meet rising electricity demand: Plan A — build a new coal-powered station; Plan B — expand the Muppandal-style wind farm already operating in the region. Evaluate both plans using what the chapter says about resource type, environmental impact, and responsible consumption. Conclude with a justified recommendation.
look_for: Correctly classifies coal as a non-renewable resource (formed over millions of years from ancient organisms) and wind energy as renewable (replenished continuously by natural processes).
Traces the impact chain for Plan A: burning coal releases smoke and carbon dioxide, contributing to air pollution and reducing air quality established as essential for life.
Notes that coal exists in limited quantities, so Plan A accelerates depletion of a finite resource.
Evaluates Plan B as harnessing a renewable resource with no combustion pollution, consistent with the chapter's examples of windmill farms generating electricity responsibly.
Makes a justified recommendation that explicitly names at least one resource-type criterion and one impact criterion from the chapter rather than expressing only a personal preference.
Optionally references the need-versus-greed principle or the chapter's call to reduce dependence on fossil fuels through available alternatives.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who find continuous evaluative writing difficult may present their response as an annotated comparison table (Plan A vs Plan B across resource type, pollution impact, and long-term supply) before writing a one-sentence recommendation — this structure scaffolds the same evaluative reasoning in a format accessible to a wider range of writers.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Scenario | Problem substance (acidic/basic/other) | Resource(s) involved | Renewable or non-renewable | Corrective or conservation action | Nature of action (reduces waste / shifts to renewable / restores resource)
A farmer's well runs dry in summer because the water table has dropped. | | | | |
A neighbourhood switches from wood-burning chulhas to solar cookers. | | | | |
A factory dumps waste into a river, making the water unsuitable for drinking. | | | | |
A state government plants trees along roads every July as part of Van Mahotsav. | | | | |
A mobile phone manufacturer designs phones using fewer mineral components. | | | | |
A village installs a Bawadi-style stepwell to collect rainwater. | | | | |
assessment_items.task: Refer to the table provided. For each scenario: (1) identify the resource(s) involved, (2) classify each resource as renewable or non-renewable, (3) propose a corrective or conservation action grounded in the chapter, and (4) state the nature of that action — whether it reduces waste, shifts dependence to a renewable resource, or works to restore a degraded resource.
assessment_items.scaffold: Use the chapter's examples and frameworks to complete each row. You may refer to your resource survey table, your fuel classification notes, and the causal chain diagrams from earlier activities. For the nature of action column, choose one of the three types given in the column header — you may also explain in a phrase if the action fits more than one type.
format_of_output: Completed table with all six rows filled in
One paragraph (3–5 sentences) after the table explaining which scenario you consider the most urgent resource problem and why, using at least one piece of evidence from the chapter.

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Classification or sorting task with justification
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The final stage LO requires students to classify resource type, trace impact chains, and justify conservation judgements simultaneously across multiple resources — a classification-with-justification table is the most natural vehicle because it externalises all three operations in a structured, observable form.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response demonstrates that the student can apply the renewable/non-renewable classification framework across diverse resource types, trace the conservation logic in real scenarios drawn from the chapter, and produce a reasoned evaluative judgement prioritising one scenario over others with evidence.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The table structure separates the three cognitive operations the LO requires — identification, classification, and evaluation of action — so teachers can diagnose which operation a student has mastered and which needs further development by reading across the columns for each student. The paragraph prompt requires the integration step: students must weigh scenarios against each other rather than treating each in isolation.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses correctly classify all six resources, propose actions that match the chapter's own examples or logic (not invented external solutions), and use the three action-type categories accurately — for instance, distinguishing 'reduces waste' (turning off a tap) from 'shifts to renewable' (solar cooker). The paragraph cites a specific chapter fact (formation timescale, pollution type, replenishment rate) as the basis for urgency. Weak responses classify resources without citing evidence, propose generic actions ('save the environment'), or confuse action types (labelling tree planting as 'shifts to renewable' rather than 'restores resource').
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find the paragraph challenging may instead write three bullet points — one fact about the chosen scenario, one reason it is urgent, and one chapter-based action — which demonstrates the same evaluative reasoning in a shorter, more accessible format. Students who complete all six rows accurately but write a minimal paragraph should still receive full credit for the classification component.
